claims.text: Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling induces a critical level of lattice strain in CoCrFeNiTi powder.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces sufficient grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi powder.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the energy barrier for a metastable FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
Spark plasma sintering at 1000°C enables full densification of the milled CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Spark plasma sintering at 1000°C suppresses excessive HCP precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Titanium drives HCP precipitation in this CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Valence electron concentration and atomic-radius mismatch govern BCC versus FCC phase stability in the proposed transition.
Mechanical alloying creates a high density of lattice defects and a nanocrystalline grain size.
The milling-induced defects and nanocrystalline structure provide a driving force for the phase transition and densification.
The rapid SPS thermal cycle supplies enough atomic diffusion for densification.
The rapid SPS cycle does not provide enough time or thermal energy for substantial Ti-driven HCP nucleation and growth.
The proposed treatment will produce a predominantly BCC or mixed FCC/BCC microstructure with minimal HCP content.
The proposed treatment will significantly increase Vickers hardness through grain-boundary strengthening and retained lattice strain.
Cast CoCrFeNiTi or CoCrFeNiTi sintered without prior milling typically has lower hardness and higher porosity than the proposed material.
Temperatures above approximately 1000°C are likely to cross a boundary at which grain growth becomes dominant or HCP precipitation becomes thermodynamically favored over BCC.
Insufficient milling duration fails to stabilize the high-energy state needed for the proposed transition.
Low-load Vickers testing at 10–50 g can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
